title: Harvest Moon and Saturn Team Up in the Night Sky This Weekend
summary:
One of the most famous full moons of the year will climb into the eastern sky this weekend. The Harvest Moon — the full moon closest to the September equinox — will rise on Saturday, Sept. 26, with Saturn shining nearby. You'll get another chance to see it on Sunday, Sept. 27.

The moon will be officially full at 12:49 p.m. EDT on Saturday, but the best view is at moonrise where you are. It will appear in the constellation Pisces. Saturn will rise just beneath it, bright enough to see without a telescope. Binoculars or a backyard telescope will give you an even crisper view of both.

Why is it called the Harvest Moon? Around the Northern Hemisphere's autumnal equinox, the moon's path meets the eastern horizon at a shallow angle. That geometry reduces the day-to-day shift in moonrise times. Instead of rising about 50 minutes later each night, the moon rises only about 25 minutes later. The result is a string of evenings with bright moonlight arriving soon after sunset. Before electric lighting, farmers used that extra light to harvest crops — hence the name.

This year, the Harvest Moon also coincides with the Mid-Autumn Festival, celebrated in Chinese and Vietnamese communities on the day of the Harvest Moon.

To get the best view, find a spot with an unobstructed view of the eastern horizon. The next full moon, the Hunter's Moon, will occur on Oct. 25 or 26, depending on your time zone. It will also be a supermoon, appearing larger and brighter than average. So step outside this weekend — the sky is putting on a show.
why_it_matters: The night sky works like a shared calendar: for thousands of years farmers, sailors and festivals all depended on the Moon's rhythms, and the Harvest Moon still ties astronomy to harvest traditions. Yet for many people living in bright cities, light pollution means a sky like this is rarely seen clearly — so events like this raise the question of what we lose when we lose the dark.

background_read: An equinox — from Latin words meaning 'equal night' — happens twice a year, around late September and late March, when the Sun sits directly above Earth's equator and day and night are almost the same length nearly everywhere. The Harvest Moon is the full moon nearest the September equinox, and it got its name because of geometry: the moon's path meets the horizon at a shallow angle, so moonrise comes only about 25 minutes later each evening instead of the usual 50, giving several nights of bright light soon after sunset.

Saturn, the sixth planet from the Sun, is famous for its bright rings and is currently visible in the evening sky as a steady golden point of light; unlike stars, planets barely twinkle. Pisces is a faint constellation — a pattern of stars that people long ago connected into a shape — whose name means 'fish'.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, celebrated in Chinese and Vietnamese communities, is a harvest holiday tied to the full moon, when families gather, eat mooncakes and look at the Moon. Sky-watchers also use the word supermoon for a full moon that happens when the Moon is near the closest point in its orbit, making it look a little larger and brighter than average.

perspectives.description: Sky-watchers, families and photographers get an easy, free show: a bright full moon with a visible planet needs no equipment, and the Mid-Autumn Festival gives the night a cultural meaning that goes beyond astronomy.

For people in cities the view may be a letdown, since light pollution can wash out faint constellations like Pisces. Whether the weekend lives up to the headlines depends on local weather, and many readers may never get the clear eastern horizon the article recommends.

The Harvest Moon's fame is really about geometry and history. The shorter gap between moonrises mattered enormously in an agricultural world without electric light, so the name preserves a farming calendar that most people no longer live by.

The Hunter's Moon later in October will be a supermoon, so moon-watching continues into the autumn. Astronomers hope popular events like this also build support for protecting dark skies from light pollution.
